name: Kyoto
tagline: Imperial temples, tea ritual and lacquered restraint.
bestMonths: Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Oct and Nov
whenBlurb: Come for cherry blossom in early April or the koyo autumn colour of mid-to-late November; skip the hot, humid rains of June to August.

ourTake.lede: Base yourself here for at least three nights and treat the famous temples as dawn or dusk affairs, Fushimi Inari and Arashiyama's bamboo are transformed before 7am and unbearable by ten. The real Kyoto is in its ryokan dinners, tea houses and the machiya backstreets of the north, not the coach-park headline sights. Skip the packaged 'geisha spotting' in Gion; book a proper ozashiki evening through your hotel instead.
ourTake.comeIf: You want temples, tea houses and ryokan quiet, and you value ritual and restraint over spectacle.
ourTake.skipIf: You need beaches, nightlife, or reliable Indian food, or you are travelling with restless young children.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: HOTEL THE MITSUI KYOTO
items.description: Built on the Mitsui family's own 300-year estate facing Nijo Castle, entered through the clan's restored landmark gate, with an Andre Fu interior and a private thermal-spring spa beneath.

items.name: Aman Kyoto
items.description: An Aman sanctuary hidden in a mossy forest garden at the foot of Mount Hidari-Daimonji, pavilions of dark timber, silence, and a hot-spring onsen among the maples.

items.name: Tawaraya Ryokan
credentials: Widely cited as Japan's finest ryokan (Inside Kyoto; 300-year history)
items.description: Widely held to be the finest ryokan in Japan, three centuries of flawless, invisible hospitality behind a plain central-city door that has kept the world's most discerning travellers.

items.name: The Shinmonzen
items.description: A Tadao Ando-designed nine-suite house on a Gion canal, run in the manner of a private ryokan, with Jean-Georges Vongerichten's only Kyoto table downstairs.

items.name: The Ritz-Carlton, Kyoto
items.description: A low, discreet house on the Kamo River blending Western luxury with ryokan calm, river-facing rooms, a Pierre Hermé salon, and Mizuki's tempura and sushi counters within.

items.name: Four Seasons Hotel Kyoto
items.description: Wrapped around an 800-year-old pond garden once written into 'The Tale of the Heike', a serene Higashiyama estate with the celebrated Sushi Wakon counter in-house.

items.name: Park Hyatt Kyoto
items.description: Perched on the Higashiyama slope beside Kodai-ji temple, with the Yasaka Pagoda framed from the rooms and the storied Kyoto Bistro and Kyoto Cuisine Yamano within.

items.name: Hiiragiya
items.description: A sixth-generation ryokan founded in 1818, one of the 'Three Great Inns of Kyoto', where antique-filled rooms and seasonal kaiseki are served with quiet ceremony.

items.name: Six Senses Kyoto
items.description: A playful, wellness-led house in the temple quarter near Sanjusangen-do, with a serious spa, an Alchemy Bar and Heian-era design wit throughout.

items.name: Suiran, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Kyoto
items.description: A riverside retreat on the Hozu River in Arashiyama, beside the Tenryu-ji gardens and the bamboo grove, some rooms with private open-air hot-spring baths.

items.name: ROKU KYOTO, LXR Hotels & Resorts
items.description: A design-led hillside resort in the artisan quarter of Rakuhoku, built around a natural hot-spring garden pool and the Tenjin-gawa stream.

items.name: Kanamean Nishitomiya
items.description: A small Relais & Châteaux ryokan of just a dozen rooms, several with private cypress or open-air baths, serving refined Kyoto kaiseki in-room.

items.name: Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
items.description: The three-storey pavilion sheathed in gold leaf floating on its mirror pond is the single most photographed sight in Japan; go at opening to walk the circuit before the crowds. A short, flat, stroller-friendly loop that lands with children and grandparents alike.

items.name: Fushimi Inari Taisha
items.description: Head shrine of some 30,000 Inari shrines, its Senbon Torii, thousands of vermilion gates, tunnel up sacred Mount Inari. Climb even twenty minutes past the first shrine and the tour groups thin to near silence; the full loop is a two-to-three-hour hike best done at dawn or after dark, lit and open around the clock.

items.name: Kiyomizu-dera
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
items.description: The great wooden stage juts thirteen metres over the hillside on a lattice of pillars joined without a single nail, framing the whole city below. Approach through the sloping lanes of Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka; the Otowa spring beneath grants long life, love or success, pick one dipper.

items.name: Ryoan-ji Rock Garden
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
items.description: Fifteen stones set in raked white gravel that can never all be seen at once from the viewing veranda, the most famous Zen dry garden in the world. Sit on the wooden platform, say nothing, and let it work; ten quiet minutes here is the point of the whole visit.

items.name: Ginkaku-ji (Silver Pavilion)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
items.description: Never actually silvered, this refined retreat is really about its garden: a moss-carpeted grove and a startling cone and sea of raked sand called the Sea of Silver Sand. The uphill loop rewards you with a lookout over eastern Kyoto, and it anchors the north end of the Philosopher's Path.

items.name: Arashiyama Bamboo Grove
items.description: A 400-metre path where towering green stalks close overhead and the wind sets them creaking, best walked at first light before the western district wakes. Free, flat and open all day; pair it with a private rickshaw ride through the back lanes to keep the family together.

items.name: Tenryu-ji
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
items.description: First of Kyoto's Five Great Zen temples, founded 1339, whose Sogen pond garden borrows the Arashiyama mountains as its backdrop, a masterpiece unchanged for seven centuries. The north gate opens straight onto the bamboo grove, and Jain and vegetarian families can book its Shigetsu shojin-ryori hall on the grounds.

items.name: Gion
items.description: Kyoto's storied geisha quarter of wooden ochaya teahouses, lantern-lit lanes and the willow-lined Shirakawa canal. Stroll Hanamikoji at dusk for the chance of a geiko or maiko slipping to an appointment; a discreet advisor can arrange a private ozashiki dinner with genuine performance rather than the tourist facsimile.

items.name: Pontocho Alley
items.description: A single lantern-lit lane barely wide enough for two, packed with intimate restaurants between Kamo River and Kiyamachi. From May to September the riverside houses raise noryo-yuka dining platforms over the water, book a private room facing the Kamo for a family dinner as the evening cools.

items.name: Nishiki Market
items.description: Four centuries of 'Kyoto's Kitchen', a covered arcade of some 130 stalls selling pickles, tofu, sweets, knives and matcha. A great grazing walk with kids; plenty of vegetable and tofu-based bites for veg travellers, and the perfect place to buy a hand-forged blade to carry home.

items.name: Nijo Castle
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
items.description: The Tokugawa shoguns' Kyoto seat, its Ninomaru palace famous for 'nightingale' floors that chirp underfoot to foil assassins, gilded audience halls and a strolling garden. Flat and easy for multi-generation groups; the wide grounds blaze with cherry and plum in season.

items.name: Nanzen-ji and the Suirokaku Aqueduct
items.description: A grand head temple of Rinzai Zen at the foot of the Higashiyama hills, where a red-brick Meiji-era aqueduct arches improbably through the ancient grounds. Climb the Sanmon gate for the view, then lose the crowds in the quiet subtemples, Konchi-in's garden is a hidden reward.

items.name: Philosopher's Path
items.description: A stone canal-side walk named for a professor who meditated here daily, running roughly two kilometres between Ginkaku-ji and Nanzen-ji under a canopy of cherry trees. Peak beauty in early April when petals drift on the water; strung with cafes and small temples to duck into.

items.name: Iwatayama Monkey Park
items.description: A short hillside climb to a troupe of 100-plus wild Japanese macaques roaming free, with one of the finest panoramas over Kyoto from the summit. Children love feeding them from inside the enclosed hut (roles reversed, the humans are caged); a genuinely different half-hour from another temple.

items.name: Okochi Sanso Villa
items.description: The hillside estate of a 1930s samurai-film star, with meticulous strolling gardens and teahouse lookouts over the whole city and the Hozu gorge. Entry includes matcha and a sweet in the tearoom; a serene, near-empty antidote to the bamboo-grove throng a few steps away.

items.name: Sanjusangendo
items.description: A single hall 120 metres long holding 1,001 gilded, life-sized statues of Kannon in serried ranks, an overwhelming, hushed sight found nowhere else. Photography is forbidden inside, which only sharpens the effect; wheelchair-accessible and quick to see between larger stops.

items.name: Tofuku-ji
items.description: A vast Zen monastery whose Tsutenkyo bridge floats over a valley of maples that turns to fire in November, Kyoto's premier autumn-leaf temple. Its modernist checkerboard moss-and-stone gardens are quietly radical; come at opening in peak season, as it draws serious crowds.

items.name: Daitoku-ji Temple Complex
items.description: A walled monastic town of more than twenty Zen subtemples, several with exquisite dry gardens, Daisen-in and Ryogen-in among them. The heartland of tea culture under Sen no Rikyu; wander the gravel lanes at leisure, and pause for shojin-ryori at Izusen inside the grounds.

items.name: Saiho-ji (Kokedera, the Moss Temple)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
items.description: A garden of some 120 varieties of moss under maples, so precious it admits only reserved guests who first copy a sutra or meditate before entering. Book weeks ahead by online application; the ritual, the near-empty grounds and the emerald light make it Kyoto's most exclusive garden hour.

items.name: Katsura Imperial Villa
items.description: The 17th-century imperial retreat revered by modernist architects worldwide as the purest expression of Japanese design, a stroll garden choreographed shot by shot around a central pond. Visits are by advance reservation and guided tour only; a connoisseur's pilgrimage rather than a casual stop.

items.name: Kyoto Imperial Palace and Gyoen Garden
items.description: The former seat of the emperor, its ceremonial halls set inside a huge gravel-and-pine park open free to all. The surrounding Gyoen is a favourite local promenade, weeping cherries in spring, cool shade in summer, and easy, flat walking for every generation.

items.name: Shugakuin Imperial Villa
items.description: A sprawling 17th-century mountainside retreat of three garden levels, the upper terrace opening onto a borrowed-scenery panorama of the northern hills and the city beyond. Reservation-only guided visits keep numbers low; the long walk between gardens through working rice paddies is part of the magic.

items.name: Ninna-ji
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
items.description: A former imperial monastery with a five-storey pagoda, palatial residence and a grove of late-blooming dwarf 'Omuro' cherries that extend the sakura season into mid-April. Spacious and unhurried compared with the marquee temples nearby; the palace's painted screens and garden veranda reward a slow visit.

items.name: Ryoan-ji's neighbour Myoshin-ji
items.description: The largest Rinzai Zen temple compound in Japan, 40-plus subtemples along stone lanes, most closed to the public but a handful open for a garden or a soaring cloud-dragon ceiling painting. Taizo-in offers hands-on Zen meditation and a garden lunch, an intimate experience away from the crowds.

items.name: Heian Shrine and Garden
items.description: A bold vermilion-and-green reconstruction of the old imperial palace fronted by a giant torii, its real treasure a circling garden famous for weeping cherries mirrored in the pond. Broad, flat paths make it easy for elders and children; a striking colour break from the muted temple palette.

items.name: Kennin-ji
items.description: Kyoto's oldest Zen temple, tucked at the foot of Gion, with a thundering twin-dragon ceiling painting and Tawaraya Sotatsu's celebrated Wind and Thunder Gods screen. Rarely crowded despite its central spot; sit on the veranda over the dry garden for a still moment between geisha-quarter lanes.

items.name: Chion-in
items.description: Headquarters of Pure Land Buddhism, entered through the largest wooden gate in Japan, with a 74-tonne bell that seventeen monks swing by rope each New Year. The scale is cinematic; the hillside setting above Maruyama Park makes it an easy pairing with Gion below.

items.name: Maruyama Park
items.description: Kyoto's oldest public park and its most beloved cherry-blossom spot, centred on a great weeping sakura lit up after dark in spring. A natural pause between Yasaka Shrine, Chion-in and Kodai-ji; benches, ponds and food stalls make it comfortable for a multi-generation afternoon.

items.name: Yasaka Shrine
items.description: The lantern-hung guardian shrine at the head of Gion, glowing at night and the beating heart of the July Gion Matsuri, one of Japan's grandest festivals. Free and always open; walk up through it from Shijo to begin an evening in the geisha district.

items.name: Kodai-ji
items.description: A refined temple built in memory of the warlord Hideyoshi, with lacquerwork halls, a bamboo grove and gardens staged for dramatic seasonal night illuminations in spring and autumn. The reflecting pond doubles the maples; an evening visit here is one of Higashiyama's quiet luxuries.

items.name: Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka Lanes
credentials: Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings
items.description: Two preserved stone-stepped streets of Meiji-era wooden shophouses climbing toward Kiyomizu-dera, the postcard image of old Kyoto. Browse ceramics, sweets and incense; families often rent kimono here for the walk, and a private guide can steer you into the crafts workshops behind the frontages.

items.name: Nishijin Textile Center
items.description: The showcase of Kyoto's 1,200-year silk-weaving tradition, with live loom demonstrations and daily kimono shows in the historic weaving district. Free to enter; a good, air-conditioned stop with children, and the launchpad for arranging a private atelier visit to a working obi weaver.

items.name: Raku Museum
items.description: A small, serious museum devoted to Raku tea bowls, the hand-shaped, low-fired ceramics made by one family for fifteen generations across 450 years. For anyone drawn to the tea ceremony or to wabi-sabi imperfection, an unmissable and blessedly quiet half-hour in the Nishijin district.

items.name: Kyoto National Museum
items.description: The city's great repository of Buddhist sculpture, painting, calligraphy and ceramics, split between a red-brick 1895 hall and a Yoshio Taniguchi-designed modern wing. Well-labelled in English and fully accessible; the essential grounding for the temples you will see across town.

items.name: Nomura Art Museum
items.description: A jewel-box collection of tea-ceremony utensils, Noh masks and costumes assembled by a finance magnate, including seven Important Cultural Properties. Small, refined and rarely busy, near Nanzen-ji; a rewarding stop for collectors and anyone deepening their interest in chanoyu.

items.name: Shigetsu Shojin-Ryori
items.description: Zen Buddhist vegetarian cuisine served on the grounds of Tenryu-ji, entirely plant-based and built around seasonal Kyoto vegetables, tofu and yuba. A rare set-course meal that Jain and vegetarian families can eat with complete confidence; reserve at least three days ahead.

items.name: Tea Ceremony at Camellia (Chado)
items.description: An English-guided chanoyu ceremony in a machiya near Kiyomizu-dera, where a host prepares matcha for you and explains each gesture, approachable without being touristy. Private and family sessions can be arranged; a gentle, seated introduction to Kyoto's defining ritual.

items.name: Kamo River Banks (Kamogawa)
items.description: The city's green spine, grassy banks where locals picnic, jog and court, spanned by stepping-stone crossings that delight children. Walk it at golden hour from Sanjo to Demachiyanagi; in summer the Pontocho restaurants above open their riverside dining decks.

items.name: Kyoto Railway Museum
items.description: A huge, hands-on museum of steam locomotives, a working roundhouse and a train simulator, with a short steam-hauled ride on weekends. The reliable rainy-day and multi-generation winner in a city of temples; grandparents and grandchildren tend to be equally delighted.

items.name: Fushimi Sake District
items.description: One of Japan's great sake towns, its soft spring water lining a canal quarter of white-walled breweries you can tour and taste; Gekkeikan's Okura museum tells the whole story. Glide the willow-lined waterway by little Jikkokubune boat, an easy, atmospheric afternoon south of the centre.

items.name: Toei Kyoto Studio Park (Uzumasa Eigamura)
items.description: A working samurai-film backlot turned theme park, with Edo streetscapes, live ninja and sword shows and costume dress-up. Unashamedly fun and squarely aimed at families; a lively counterweight for children after a run of temples and gardens.

items.name: Nara Day Trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara
items.description: Japan's first permanent capital, an easy 45 minutes away, where 1,200 free-roaming sacred deer bow for crackers and Todai-ji's great hall shelters the world's largest bronze Buddha. Add the lantern-lined path to Kasuga Taisha; flat, walkable and endlessly charming for children.

items.name: Uji Day Trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto
items.description: Twenty minutes south, the home of Japan's finest matcha and of Byodo-in, whose Phoenix Hall floats on its pond and adorns the ten-yen coin. Grind your own tea, walk the riverside setting of The Tale of Genji, and lunch on matcha everything, a serene, uncrowded half-day.

items.name: Kurama and Kibune Day Trip
items.description: A retro mountain railway climbs 30 minutes north to the mystical Kurama-dera, from which a forest trail crosses the ridge down to Kibune's shrine and stream. In summer, dine on kawadoko platforms suspended over the rushing river; soak afterwards at Kurama Onsen, the coolest escape from the city heat.

items.name: Ohara and Sanzen-in
items.description: A pastoral valley an hour north where the moss gardens and Amida hall of Sanzen-in feel a world away from central Kyoto. Deeply seasonal, hydrangeas in June, maples in November, and blissfully quiet; a soft, rural day for travellers who have already ticked the icons.

items.name: Kifune Shrine
items.description: A shrine to the water deity reached by a photogenic stone stair flanked by red lanterns, where you draw fortunes that surface only when floated on the sacred spring water. A short, evocative stop that pairs naturally with the Kurama-Kibune hike and riverside dining.

items.name: Kikunoi Honten
items.description: The temple of Kyoto kaiseki, third-generation chef Yoshihiro Murata's seasonal poetry on a plate, three stars unbroken since the guide reached Kyoto.

items.name: Hyotei
items.description: Four centuries and fourteen generations beside Nanzen-ji temple, the birthplace of the famous soft-boiled 'Hyotei egg' and the soul of Kyoto minimalism.

items.name: Gion Sasaki
items.description: Hiroshi Sasaki's exuberant, playful kaiseki performed around an open counter, tradition with a showman's flourish, and among the hardest seats in Gion.

items.name: Isshisoden Nakamura
items.description: Sixth-generation chef Motokazu Nakamura keeps Kyoto's refined imperial-court cuisine alive, subtle seasoning, centuries of technique, three stars.

items.name: Gion Maruyama
items.description: An intimate Gion counter where chef Masayoshi Maruyama's precise, seasonal kaiseki has held two stars, quiet mastery in the geisha quarter.

items.name: Gion Nishikawa
items.description: Restrained, exact kaiseki from chef Masayoshi Nishikawa, a serene Gion room and dashi of remarkable clarity.

items.name: Gion Matayoshi
items.description: A tiny, focused Gion room where chef Hitoshi Matayoshi cooks a deeply seasonal kaiseki with rare purity, two stars, and only a handful of seats.

items.name: Higashiyama Yoshihisa
items.description: Chef Yoshihisa's exacting seasonal Japanese cuisine near the Higashiyama slopes, a composed, two-star counter of quiet confidence.

items.name: Sanso Kyoyamato
items.description: Kyoto kaiseki since 1877 in a grand old villa wrapped in a pristine garden beside Kodai-ji temple, newly raised to two stars.

items.name: Higashiyama Ogata
items.description: Chef Toshiro Ogata's serene, produce-driven kaiseki in a hushed Higashiyama room, a deeply personal, meditative meal.

items.name: Kikunoi Roan
items.description: The Kikunoi family's more relaxed riverside counter on Kiyamachi, the same seasonal artistry as the flagship, in a lighter register.

items.name: Cenci
items.description: Chef Ken Sakamoto's Italian cooking read through a Kyoto lens, local, seasonal produce, a strong vegetable-forward opening, and one of the city's most exciting rooms.

items.name: Jean-Georges at The Shinmonzen
items.description: Jean-Georges Vongerichten's only Kyoto table, on a Gion canal inside the Tadao Ando-designed Shinmonzen, his signature light French touch, Kyoto ingredients.

items.name: Honke Tankuma Honten
items.description: A century-old Kyoto institution serving classical kaiseki in a beautiful old machiya townhouse, tradition kept exactly as it should be.

items.name: Gion Iwasaki
items.description: A refined, seasonal Gion counter where the kaiseki is precise and unhurried, a quietly excellent one-star in the heart of the old quarter.

items.name: Kappo Hassun
items.description: Warm, counter-style kappo cooking in Gion, seasonal Kyoto dishes served with easy conversation across the counter.

items.name: Hiramatsu Kodaiji
items.description: Refined French dining in a converted old house beside Kodai-ji temple, garden views, a graceful room, and one Michelin star.

items.name: HANA-Kitcho
items.description: The Kitcho lineage's Kyoto kaiseki, seasonal, classical Japanese cuisine from one of the great names in the tradition, at one star.

items.name: Vegan Ramen UZU
items.description: A teamLab-designed room serving fully plant-based ramen of real depth, proof that Kyoto's vegetarian craft runs deep.

items.name: K6
credentials: Long-regarded as one of Kyoto's leading authentic bars (Wine Enthusiast)
items.description: An elegant, spirits-deep second-floor bar overlooking the Takase canal, a vast whisky and spirits backbar and classical technique, long a Kyoto institution.

items.name: The Bar (The Ritz-Carlton, Kyoto)
items.description: A polished riverside hotel bar in the Ritz-Carlton, with Kyoto-accented cocktails and views over the Kamo River and the Higashiyama hills.

items.name: Bee's Knees
items.description: Toru Ariyoshi's Prohibition-era speakeasy behind a plain yellow door, Roaring-Twenties classics, theatrical service, and the most decorated bar in the city.

items.name: Nokishita711
credentials: Widely cited among Japan's most singular cocktail experiences
items.description: Tomoiki Sekine's four-seat 'liquid cuisine' counter, where drinks are built by extracting flavour from seasonal Kyoto produce rather than mixing spirits, a tasting menu in a glass.

items.name: Bar Rocking Chair
credentials: Repeatedly cited by industry pros as an essential Kyoto bar
items.description: A beloved backstreet den since 2009, mixing beautifully original cocktails from Japanese ingredients, Kyoto sansho pepper, Japanese pear, Shine muscat.

items.name: L'Escamoteur
credentials: A cornerstone of Kyoto's craft-cocktail scene
items.description: A cramped, candlelit 'magician's' bar of books, decanters and curios, where flamboyant staff serve cocktails themed on mystery and alchemy, pure theatre.

items.name: Sours (Kyoto Kissa Master)
credentials: Cited among Kyoto's essential bars by industry pros (Wine Enthusiast)
items.description: A tightly focused counter bar known for precise, produce-led sours and a serious approach to classic technique in the Nishikiyamachi nightlife lane.

items.name: Pontocho lantern lanes
credentials: One of Kyoto's most atmospheric preserved nightlife lanes
items.description: A single narrow lantern-lit alley between Shijo and Sanjo, packed with tiny bars, kappo counters and riverside kawadoko terraces glowing over the Kamo River.

plan.heading: 4 days in Kyoto, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle at the Aman Kyoto in its secluded forest, then an early walk to Kiyomizu-dera before the lanes of Higashiyama fill.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The stone paths of Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka down to Kodai-ji, with tea at a machiya teahouse.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Kaiseki at Kikunoi Honten, chef Yoshihiro Murata's three-star house, or a private table at Aman's the Living Pavilion.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The moss and raked gravel of Ryoan-ji and the gold of Kinkaku-ji, walked at opening before the crowds.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Arashiyama bamboo grove and the Okochi Sanso villa gardens, then a boat on the Hozu or tea nearby.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Gion Sasaki or the counter at Hyotei, a 400-year-old kaiseki house by Nanzen-ji.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: A private morning with a tea master, then the lacquer and textile ateliers of the Nishijin weaving district.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Fushimi Inari's vermilion gates walked in the quiet upper reaches, then a sake tasting in Fushimi.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: An arranged evening in Gion, a discreet ozashiki with geiko and maiko, then a light supper at Giro Giro Hitoshina.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: The villa gardens of Shugakuin or Katsura by advance permit, a rare and unhurried privilege.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: The Philosopher's Path to Ginkaku-ji, then the Fukuda Art Museum or a final tea by the Kamo river.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell kaiseki at Roan Kikunoi in the heart of town, then a quiet last night in the forest.

items.name: Higashiyama
items.description: The eastern temple district, best for first-timers who want to walk to Kiyomizu-dera and the lantern-lit lanes at night.

items.name: Gion & Pontocho
items.description: The old geisha quarters along the Kamo river; suits those who want restaurants, tea houses and evening atmosphere on the doorstep.

items.name: Kamigyo & the northern machiya streets
items.description: Quieter, residential, near the Imperial Palace, for repeat visitors who prefer townhouse stays over temple crowds.

events.name: Aoi Matsuri
events.note: The oldest of Kyoto's three great festivals, a Heian-era court procession in ox-carts and silk from the Imperial Palace to the Kamo shrines.

events.name: Gion Matsuri
events.note: The month-long summer festival of the Yasaka shrine, peaking with the towering Yamaboko float processions and the yoiyama street evenings before them.

events.name: Jidai Matsuri
events.note: The 'Festival of the Ages', a costumed pageant marching a thousand years of Japanese history through the streets.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Book a night or two in a fine ryokan for the kaiseki-and-onsen ritual; visit the marquee temples at opening or dusk to avoid crowds, and in Gion photograph geiko discreetly and never block their path, as private streets are now off-limits to unescorted visitors.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Osaka's Kansai International (KIX) and take a private car for the roughly 90-minute transfer, or arrive elegantly by Shinkansen from Tokyo into Kyoto Station in about two hours fifteen.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private car and driver suits the spread-out temples; central districts like Gion and Higashiyama are made for unhurried walking.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Ubigi or Airalo) works throughout; hotel and ryokan wifi is dependable.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Japanese yen (JPY); cards are accepted at hotels and larger venues, but carry cash for temples, teahouses and smaller shops, and there is no tipping.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Spring (late March-April cherry blossom) and autumn (November foliage) are unmatched here. Avoid June's rains and the July-August summer, hills on three sides trap the heat and humidity, making it feel hotter than Tokyo, often into September.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Kyoto has no airport; fly into Osaka Kansai (KIX), reached direct from Delhi (and via a hub from Mumbai/Bengaluru) or one-stop through Tokyo Haneda on ANA/JAL/Air India. From KIX the JR Haruka limited express reaches Kyoto Station in about 75-90 minutes, or a private car in similar time, arrange the transfer ahead as station navigation with luggage is tedious.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; exceptionally safe and orderly. Tap water is clean and drinkable. The only real caution is heat exhaustion if you come in high summer.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Kyoto is the home of shojin-ryori, refined Buddhist vegetarian cuisine, which suits Jain and pure-veg travellers beautifully, though still confirm no dashi. Dedicated Indian restaurants are fewer than in Tokyo, so book shojin temples (Shigetsu at Tenryu-ji is exceptional) and let a good hotel source Indian when wanted.
